title: Mark Twain on Formal Schooling: 'Never Let Schooling Interfere with Your Education'
summary: Addressing students and professors, American humorist Mark Twain offered his timeless satirical counsel on why authentic education requires thinking beyond rigid classrooms.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 195: நேருவும் அதிகாரச் சமநிலை பற்றிய எதிர்கேள்வியும்
full_text:
At the turn of the twentieth century, the commencement hall of a prominent American university was packed with faculty draped in academic velvet and eager graduates clutching diplomas.

The guest of honor was Samuel L. Clemens, known to the world as Mark Twain. Striding to the podium in his immaculate white linen suit, Twain surveyed the rows of solemn academics and launched into an address of sparkling, iconoclastic wisdom:

"Young ladies and gentlemen, you have listened to hours of solemn advice urging you to revere your academic degrees. But as an old traveler who has navigated the river of human experience, let me leave you with one vital rule of life:
'I have never let my schooling interfere with my education!'

Schoolrooms and lecture halls are useful for teaching you grammar, arithmetic, and how to pass examinations. But do not confuse the syllabus with wisdom! True education begins outside these four brick walls in the vast, turbulent laboratory of human society.
Education is the capacity to think critically for yourself, to question entrenched dogmas, to feel genuine empathy for the downtrodden, and to look upon pomposity with a discerning chuckle. A diploma is merely a receipt stating that you paid your tuition fees—your real education begins when you start learning from life itself!"

The students erupted into delighted cheers while professors smiled ruefully. Twain gave voice to the timeless truth that rote formal instruction is only a prelude to lifelong intellectual independence.
